column1: Why does fermentation yield only ~2 ATP per glucose molecule compared to ~32 ATP in aerobic respiration?
column2: Without oxygen as terminal electron acceptor, cells rely solely on substrate-level phosphorylation during glycolysis, forgoing the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.

column1: What is the metabolic purpose of converting pyruvate to ethanol via acetaldehyde in yeast fermentation?
column2: It regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH, allowing glycolysis to continue producing ATP under anaerobic conditions.

column1: What are the two endogenous amylases in flour and what do they each do?
column2: Alpha-amylase cleaves internal glycosidic bonds in starch chains; beta-amylase liberates maltose from non-reducing ends of starch chains.

column1: State the foundational invariant equation of leavening.
column2: Final product volume = gas produced × fraction of gas retained by the structural matrix, modulated by temperature and pressure conditions.

column1: What three variables control the degree of gluten development in a dough?
column2: Flour protein content, hydration percentage (baker's percentage), and mechanical energy input (kneading/folding).

column1: How do biological and chemical leaveners differ in gas production mechanism and flavor impact?
column2: Biological leaveners (yeast/sourdough) produce CO2 via slow metabolic fermentation with flavor byproducts (ethanol, acids, esters); chemical leaveners (baking soda/powder) produce CO2 via fast acid-base or thermal reactions that are flavor-neutral.

column1: What is the optimal temperature range for Saccharomyces cerevisiae activity in dough, and what happens above 46°C?
column2: Optimal range is 24°C–29°C; above 46°C the yeast dies, and above 35°C it experiences thermal stress producing off-flavors.
The temporal window during which dough maintains optimal handling characteristics and baking performance before enzymatic degradation and gas cell coalescence degrade structure.

column1: Why does a high-hydration ciabatta (80%) have a much shorter fermentation tolerance than a stiff bagel dough (55%)?
column2: High hydration doughs have less structural resistance, so enzymatic degradation and gas cell coalescence destroy structure faster (15-30 min window) vs. stiffer doughs with strengtheners tolerating ~2 hours.

column1: What are the three classical heat transfer mechanisms active simultaneously during bread baking, and which layer does each primarily govern?
column2: Convective heat (oven air/steam) strikes the outer surface; conductive heat travels inward through the crumb matrix; radiant heat (deck/Dutch oven walls) penetrates base and sides intensely.

column1: Why does removing a Dutch oven lid at the 20-minute mark redirect baking energy toward browning rather than oven spring?
column2: By that point internal structure has set enough to stop expanding, so the sudden convective dry heat from removing the lid focuses energy on surface Maillard browning instead of further rise.

column1: What are the triple-confirmation criteria for a sourdough levain being ready to use, per the lab protocol?
column2: Volume rise to at least 2.5×–3× original, pH at or below 4.2, and a positive float test (floats within 30 seconds in still water) — all three must confirm simultaneously.
